extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of European/Napoleonic history
extracted.subtask_description: Compose narrative histories of political and military events that combine chronological facts with interpretive, rhetorical commentary and illustrative anecdotes. Emphasizes characterization of leaders, causal analysis, and documentary support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vivid characterisation of leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray principal figures with strong, memorable character judgments and striking phrases (e.g., Napoleon 'possessed and tormented by the demon of war', 'the little hat of the Corsican').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concentrated, evaluative language and telling anecdotes (seizure of the Duc d'Enghien, self-coronation, family appointments) to make leadership personalities vivid and consequential. Contrast public role and private motive to illuminate character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anchor narrative in precise dates and events
rubrics_metrics.description: Anchor claims and narrative turns with exact dates and named engagements (e.g., 'On the 18th of May, 1804', 'the battle ... at Austerlitz ... on the 2d of December, 1805').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide chronological markers and specific place-names to orient the reader and substantiate causal sequences; list treaties, proclamations, and campaign dates when introducing major shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral and evaluative commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Interleave factual narrative with explicit moral judgments and interpretive claims (e.g., liberty 'had ceased to be in vogue', France 'to be enriched by the plunder of her neighbors').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't shy from taking a stance: evaluate motives, label actions (ignominious, beneficent, servile), and use such commentary to frame the significance of events for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain causes and consequences (causal analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Trace how decisions and events produce political outcomes (e.g., Prussia's delayed declaration of war leading to strategic disadvantage; Napoleonic reorganizations dissolving the empire).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show connective logic between actions and results, identify missed opportunities and strategic errors, and make clear how local choices aggregate into systemic change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustrative anecdotes and concrete incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrate larger themes through specific, often vivid incidents (e.g., the Bernese ambassador exchange about cattle/cheese, the murder of the bookseller Palm, the shameless fraud at a Paris banquet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select short, telling episodes that exemplify broader patterns; use them as narrative anchors to humanize abstract political transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary apparatus: footnotes for sourcing and amplification
rubrics_metrics.description: Supply numerous footnotes to cite sources, give ancillary facts, or offer clarifying editorial remarks (many footnotes supply provenance, anecdotal detail, and cross-references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use endnotes/footnotes to preserve narrative flow while providing documentary support, source references, and explanatory asides for readers who want deeper context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison with historical exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame contemporary figures or events by comparing them to renowned historical models (e.g., likening Napoleon's elevation to Charlemagne; 'the standard of Charlemagne' invoked).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comparison to heighten significance and provide cultural resonance; invoke canonical figures to show continuity or profanation of tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sectioned narrative structure with clear headings
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize long treatments into numbered/chaptered sections and topical headings (e.g., 'CCLIII. Fall of the Holy Roman-Germanic Empire') to separate themes and chronological stages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break long narratives into titled sections to focus attention, aid navigation, and allow discrete arguments or episodes to be developed succinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine macro political reorganisation with administrative detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe large-scale constitutional and territorial changes alongside concrete administrative swaps and titles (e.g., which bishoprics/territories were annexed, who received which titles or lands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the factual mechanics of political change (treaties, territorial exchanges, creation/abolition of offices) to substantiate claims about systemic transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ rhetorical devices: irony, sarcasm, and epigram
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ironic or biting turns of phrase to underline critique or satire (e.g., 'the little hat of the Corsican', 'Long live Napoleon, the restorer of the kingdom of Bavaria!').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy irony and epigram to convey the author's attitude and to make prose more engaging; let pointed phrases puncture pomp or reveal absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show interplay of public policy and personal/self-interested motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate how reforms and institutions served both national aims (laws, manufactures, administration) and personal aggrandizement (placing relatives on thrones, family alliances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose dual incentives by detailing public reforms together with nepotistic appointments and dynastic marriages; let readers see policy as both statecraft and personal ambition.
